common_name: Treasure Azalea (Pink-Budded White Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Treasure is a Glenn Dale Hybrid grown for pale pink buds opening to white flowers on a reliably hardy, well-branched plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Treasure is one of the many Glenn Dale Hybrid azaleas bred by USDA horticulturist Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station in Maryland to combine cold hardiness with large, showy flowers drawn from tender Asian azalea species. It produces an abundant single flush of broad flowers that open from pale pink buds to white, often marked with small pink spots or a soft chartreuse blotch on the upper petals, over a dense, well-branched, evergreen to semi-evergreen mound reaching 3-5 feet. Its reliable floriferousness and hardiness have kept it in commerce among collectors and public gardens long after many lesser-known Glenn Dale selections faded from the trade. Water deeply during dry spells, keep mulch over the shallow root zone, and prune only right after bloom since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.

common_name: Vespers Azalea (White Green-Blotched Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Vespers is a widely grown Glenn Dale Hybrid noted for large, frilled white flowers marked with a pale yellow-green throat blotch.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Vespers is among the most enduringly popular Glenn Dale Hybrid azaleas bred by Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the USDA's Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station, prized for large, frilled white flowers softened by a pale yellow-green blotch in the throat. The plant forms an upright, well-branched evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub 3-5 feet tall and blooms in a single heavy flush in mid-to-late spring. Its dependable vigor and cold hardiness have kept it widely available at specialty nurseries long after many other Glenn Dale cultivars became hard to find. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool, and prune only right after flowering since next year's buds set soon afterward.

common_name: Joseph Hill Azalea (Red North Tisbury Groundcover Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Joseph Hill is a North Tisbury hybrid bred by Polly Hill from Rhododendron nakaharae, valued for its flat, spreading groundcover habit and late red flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Joseph Hill is a North Tisbury hybrid azalea, part of a group of low, spreading evergreen azaleas developed by Polly Hill on Martha's Vineyard from Rhododendron nakaharae crosses to bring that species' prostrate habit and unusually late bloom time into a hardier garden plant. It produces bright red flowers in early summer, well after most other azaleas have finished, on wide-spreading, trailing stems that hug the ground and root as they spread. The low, flat habit makes it a distinctive flowering groundcover for underplanting taller shrubs, draping over walls, or massing in partial shade. Prune lightly only right after bloom if needed, since flower buds set on the current season's growth.

common_name: Pink Pancake Azalea (Prostrate North Tisbury Groundcover Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Pancake is a North Tisbury hybrid bred by Polly Hill from Rhododendron nakaharae, named for its unusually flat, mat-forming habit and salmon-pink late-season flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Pink Pancake is a North Tisbury hybrid azalea bred by Polly Hill on Martha's Vineyard from Rhododendron nakaharae, selected for an exceptionally flat, ground-hugging habit even within a breeding group already known for low, spreading forms. Soft salmon-pink flowers with red spotting open in early summer, later than most other azaleas, on evergreen stems that press close to the soil and root along their length as they spread outward. Its extreme flatness makes it especially useful for draping over rock walls, cascading down slopes, or carpeting the ground beneath taller shade shrubs. Prune lightly only right after bloom if needed, since flower buds set on the current season's growth.
